"Chum" as a verb has two meanings. I'll explain both fully.
Meaning 1 — In Fishing (the primary, widely-used meaning)

When fishermen "chum" the water, they throw a mixture of chopped fish, fish blood, fish guts, and other messy, smelly organic matter into the water. The goal is to attract fish — especially large ones like sharks, tuna, or marlin — to the boat's location, making them easier to catch.

The noun "chum" is the name for that bloody, fishy mixture itself. The verb "to chum" is the act of throwing it into the water to lure fish.

The idea is simple: fish are attracted to the smell of blood and food in the water. By releasing this trail of scent and particles, a fisherman pulls fish toward the boat, almost like ringing a dinner bell underwater.

Examples:

  • "The captain chummed the water for an hour before anyone cast a line."
  • "They chummed with sardine pieces and blood, and within minutes, sharks appeared."
  • "Chumming is controversial because some say it makes sharks associate boats with food."

You'll notice "chumming" (the -ing form) is extremely common — it's often used as a noun to describe the technique itself: "Chumming is widely practiced in deep-sea fishing."
Meaning 2 — To Accompany Someone (Scottish and British English)

In Scottish English and parts of British English, "to chum" someone means to walk with them somewhere or escort them as a friendly gesture. It comes from the noun "chum" meaning a close friend, so "to chum someone" essentially means to be their companion on the way somewhere.

Examples:

  • "I'll chum you to the station." (= I'll walk with you to the station.)
  • "She chummed her friend home after the late-night party."
  • "Can you chum me to the shop? It's a bit dark outside."

This meaning is regional and informal. Outside Scotland and Britain — especially in American English — almost nobody uses the word this way. So if you encounter it, the context will usually make clear which meaning is intended.

Because of its fishing origins, you will sometimes see "chum the waters" used figuratively in writing or journalism. It means to deliberately stir things up, provoke a reaction, or attract attention — often in a calculated or manipulative way.

  • "The candidate chummed the waters with a divisive speech, knowing the media would react."
  • "That headline really chummed the waters on social media."

Think of it exactly like the fishing act: throwing something out specifically to draw a crowd or trigger a frenzy.

UseCore idea
FishingThrowing bloody bait into water to attract fish
British/ScottishAccompanying or escorting a friend somewhere
FigurativeStirring things up deliberately to attract attention or reaction

In the vast majority of cases globally, if you see "chum" or "chumming" as a verb, it's the fishing meaning. The other two uses are either regional or occasional.
